meta.title: Measured effects of ban the box: hiring, statistical discrimination, public sector, recidivism
meta.status: PARTIAL: every figure is from a page fetched Nov 8, 2026; several papers' full texts returned 403, so their figures come from abstracts or from Kaestner and Wang's summary; Craigie and Kaestner and Wang disagree on the public-sector effect (about 30% versus about 60%); the share of public applications that ask, earnings effects and recidivism effect sizes were NOT FOUND.

findings.outcome: Callback penalty of a felony record where employer still asks (no BTB)
findings.estimate: 63% higher callback for applicants without record (5.2 pp over 8.2% baseline with record)
findings.se_or_ci: employers that ask about criminal records were 63% more likely to call back an applicant if he has no record
findings.years: ~15,000 fictitious online applications to NJ and NYC employers (mostly large retail chains) with the box
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Race gap in callbacks at employers with the box, before BTB
findings.estimate: white 7% more callbacks than black (perfect-quad sample: gap 0.7 pp, 6.7%)
findings.se_or_ci: Before BTB, white applicants to employers with the box received 7% more callbacks than similar black applicants
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Race gap in callbacks at treated employers after BTB (statistical discrimination)
findings.estimate: gap rises to 45% (triple-difference 3.7 pp, 4.0 pp in perfect-quad sample); overall callback 11.7%
findings.se_or_ci: BTB increases this gap to 45%.
findings.population: triple-diff 0.0371, SE 0.0180 (Table 4 col 1), ** significant; perfect-quad 0.0399, SE 0.0200
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Callbacks for black applicants WITHOUT records at treated employers, pre vs post BTB
findings.estimate: 12.7% to 11% (-1.7 pp, 13% decrease); white without records 13.8% to 15%
findings.se_or_ci: Callback rates for black applicants without records decrease 12.7% to 11% (-1.7 pp or a 13% decrease)
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Callbacks for applicants WITH records at treated employers, pre vs post BTB
findings.estimate: black with record 8.4% to 11% (+2.6 pp, 31%); white with record 8.8% to 15% (+6.2 pp, 70%); untreated employers rose 1.3 pp
findings.se_or_ci: for white applicants with records they increase from 8.8% to 15% (+6.2 pp or a 70% increase)
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Employment of young low-skilled black men after BTB (CPS, state/local BTB mostly public-employer)
findings.estimate: -3.4 pp (-5.1% of baseline)
findings.se_or_ci: BTB policies decrease the probability of being employed by 3.4 percentage points (5.1%) for young, low-skilled black men
findings.years: men 25-34 without college degree, Black, in MSAs treated by any BTB
findings.url: Doleac & Hansen, 'Does Ban the Box Help or Hurt Low-Skilled Workers?' NBER WP 22469 (July 2016; published J. Labor Economics 38(2), 2020)

findings.outcome: Employment of young low-skilled Hispanic men after BTB
findings.se_or_ci: by 2.3 percentage points (2.9%) for young, low-skilled Hispanic men
findings.url: Doleac & Hansen, 'Does Ban the Box Help or Hurt Low-Skilled Workers?' NBER WP 22469 (July 2016; published J. Labor Economics 38(2), 2020)

findings.outcome: Employment of older (35-64) low-skilled black men after BTB
findings.se_or_ci: BTB increases black male employment by a statistically significant 2.8 percentage points (4.3%).
findings.url: Doleac & Hansen, 'Does Ban the Box Help or Hurt Low-Skilled Workers?' NBER WP 22469 (July 2016; published J. Labor Economics 38(2), 2020)

findings.outcome: Employment of low-skilled white men after BTB (benefit to whites, mechanism check)
findings.estimate: white men in group +3.9 pp (5.6%)
findings.se_or_ci: On average, white men in this group are 3.9 percentage points (5.6%) more likely
findings.url: Doleac & Hansen, 'Does Ban the Box Help or Hurt Low-Skilled Workers?' NBER WP 22469 (July 2016; published J. Labor Economics 38(2), 2020)

findings.outcome: Public-sector employment of people WITH convictions after BTB
findings.estimate: about +30% on average per the Smith abstract; the next row's review (Kaestner & Wang) reports +4 pp (about 60%). The two do not match, so use the range.
findings.se_or_ci: BTB policies raise the probability of public employment for those with convictions by about 30% on average.
findings.years: NLSY97 respondents with convictions, avg age 29
findings.url: https://scholarworks.smith.edu/eco_facpubs/68

findings.outcome: Craigie quoted by Kaestner-Wang: public job probability for those with convictions
findings.estimate: +4 pp, 'about 60%'
findings.se_or_ci: a BTB law increased the probability of holding a public sector job by four percentage points, or about 60%.
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Statistical discrimination test in Craigie (triple-difference)
findings.estimate: no evidence of statistical discrimination against young low-skilled minority males
findings.se_or_ci: uncovers no evidence to support the hypothesis
findings.url: Craigie 2020 (Smith College abstract)

findings.outcome: Employment in high-crime neighborhoods after BTB; public sector largest
findings.estimate: up to +4% employment of residents; 'particularly large in the public sector' and lower-wage jobs
findings.se_or_ci: increased employment of residents in high-crime neighborhoods by up to 4 percent
findings.years: residents of high-crime neighborhoods, nationwide local/state BTB
findings.url: Shoag & Veuger, 'Ban-the-Box Measures Help High-Crime Neighborhoods', J. Law & Economics 64(1), 2021

findings.outcome: Massachusetts BTB (all employers) employment of people with arrest records
findings.se_or_ci: associated with a two to three percentage point (four to six percent) decrease in employment among those with a criminal record
findings.population: not extracted; KW notes parallel-trends assumption questionable
findings.years: people with arrest record (convictions and non), Massachusetts
findings.url: Jackson & Zhao (2017), as reported in Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Seattle 2013 BTB (all employers) effect on ex-offenders
findings.estimate: negligible / no significant employment effect; convictions themselves cut employment and earnings
findings.se_or_ci: had negligible impacts on ex-offenders' labor market outcomes
findings.url: Rose, 'Does Banning the Box Help Ex-Offenders Get Jobs?', J. Labor Economics 2021 (abstract via Semantic Scholar API)

findings.outcome: Re-estimate of Doleac-Hansen with ACS and corrected law coding
findings.estimate: no discrimination: employment effects near zero, precisely estimated
findings.se_or_ci: we find no evidence of BTB-related discrimination: employment effects are near zero, precisely estimated
findings.population: precisely estimated near zero (numbers not in fetched abstract)
findings.url: Burton & Wasser, 'Revisiting the unintended consequences of Ban the Box', J. Public Economics 2025 (SSRN 4910518 abstract via Crossref API)

findings.outcome: Any BTB law, all employers, 2004-2019, young Black men
findings.se_or_ci: no systematic or statistically significant association with employment of low-educated men, both young and old
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: State and local public-sector BTB laws, effect on young Black men's employment
findings.estimate: no statistically significant or economically meaningful effect
findings.se_or_ci: had no statistically significant or economically meaningful effect on this type of employment among young Black men
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Coverage of BTB by employer type
findings.estimate: by 2019 ~26% of low-educated men 25-34 covered by private-employer BTB; 45% by law covering all public-sector jobs
findings.se_or_ci: approximately 26% of low-educated men aged 25 to 34 are covered by a BTB law applicable to private employment and 45%
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Public sector share of employment (scale of treated jobs)
findings.estimate: less than 5% of all employment (authors' statement)
findings.se_or_ci: employment in the public sector is less than 5% all employment
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Recidivism: BTB at release and re-offending
findings.estimate: no overall reduction; higher recidivism for black ex-offenders released into BTB labor market, little/no effect for whites
findings.se_or_ci: associated with higher rates of recidivism for black ex-offenders, with little to no effect for white ex-offenders
findings.population: effect sizes not in fetched abstract
findings.url: Sherrard, ''Ban the Box' Policies and Criminal Recidivism', SSRN 2020 (abstract via Semantic Scholar API)

findings.outcome: BTB and crime (arrests)
findings.estimate: +10% in criminal incidents involving Hispanic male arrestees; no increase in property crime among African American men
findings.se_or_ci: BTB laws are associated with a 10 percent increase in criminal incidents involving Hispanic male arrestees
findings.paper: state/local BTB laws, years not in fetched snippet
findings.url: Sabia, Mackay, Nguyen & Dave, 'Do Ban the Box Laws Increase Crime?' NBER WP 24381 (2018, rev. 2020)

findings.outcome: Population affected: adults with a criminal record
findings.estimate: 70 million adults (media estimate); 64% of unemployed men by age 35 have an arrest, 46% a conviction (Bushway et al. 2022)
findings.se_or_ci: A frequent estimate found in the media is that 70 million adults have a criminal record
findings.url: Kaestner & Wang, 'Ban-the-Box Laws: Fair and Effective?' NBER WP 32273 (Mar 2024)

findings.outcome: Population affected: felony conviction by race
findings.estimate: 25% of US black population vs 6% of non-black population (Shannon et al. 2011, cited); arrest by 23: 49% of black men vs 38% of white men (Brame et al. 2014, cited)
findings.se_or_ci: Shannon et al. (2011) estimate that 25% of the U.S. black population has a felony conviction, compared with only 6%
findings.url: Agan & Starr, 'Ban the Box, Criminal Records, and Statistical Discrimination: A Field Experiment' (Aug 2016 working-paper version fetched; published QJE 133(1), 2018, doi 10.1093/qje/qjx028)

findings.outcome: Reach of BTB policies
findings.estimate: 37 states and over 150 cities and counties; 37 states apply to public-sector employment; over 267 million people (more than four-fifths) live in covered jurisdictions
findings.se_or_ci: over 267 million people in the United States—more than four-fifths of the U.S. population—live in a jurisdiction
findings.url: Avery & Lu, NELP, 'Ban the Box: U.S. Cities, Counties, and States Adopt Fair Hiring Policies'

findings.outcome: Federal and state coverage as of 2015
findings.estimate: 34 states and DC had BTB by Dec 2015; federal jobs banned the box late 2015
findings.se_or_ci: similar policies exist in 34 states and the District of Columbia
findings.url: Doleac & Hansen, 'Does Ban the Box Help or Hurt Low-Skilled Workers?' NBER WP 22469 (July 2016; published J. Labor Economics 38(2), 2020)
